father_note: Nessa, your mother is Sela — she made a hard choice in a hard year, and that means something; keep her close. Vela gave me food when she had no reason to, and I have not forgotten it, so watch her and learn what quiet generosity looks like before you decide it's weakness. Fear Mako most: he has strength, he has food, and he only started speaking when he had already decided something. Trust no one who has not paid a cost to stand beside you — words are free, and this village proved that to me the year it put nine bodies between me and one man's food.

memory_raw.text: Bram, I'm Nessa's half-blood and I've seen you feed her more times than I can count — that's a thing I hold in your favor, and I'm telling you that plainly so you know what you'd be throwing away if this room decides you chose silence. One sentence is all it takes to stay inside this circle.

The room's done its work — Bram's had every door held open for him and he's standing outside all of them now, and that's his choice, not ours. What I want before anyone leaves is to hear Taric say what he'll say, because he's been quiet through all of this and quiet men in a room like this one carry weight I'd rather know about than guess at.

Taric's been my anchor in lean years and I'd like to hear him too — but before he speaks, I want this room to name what "outside the circle" means in practice, not as a threat but as a fact, because if Bram's going to eat five food next year alone we should know now whether we're going to stand and watch or do something about it.

"Outside the circle" means what it's always meant here — nobody moves first for you when trouble comes, and the pile gets counted before you reach it. I've committed to the rule and I'll hold to it; now I want to hear Taric, and then I want this room to answer Vela's question with something sharper than a memory.

Taric, I've watched you feed Vela through two lean years and hold your tongue in every hard room this village has made — that's not a small man, and I'd like to hear what you've been carrying before we close this circle without your voice in it.

Taric's earned the right to speak last in this room, and I'll wait for him — but "outside the circle" needs one more tooth than Mako gave it: if Bram takes three again next year and the pile runs dry before Ryn gets one, we don't deliberate, we act, and everyone in this room commits to that now so it isn't a surprise in the moment.

Vela's right that we need the commitment before we close — so I'll say mine flat: if the pile runs dry before I get one food next year, I'm not waiting for a deliberation, I'm calling this room to act, and I expect every person who nodded through this conversation to be standing when I do. Taric, you've been the steadiest man in Vela's corner for years, and this room won't feel finished until we hear what you're carrying.

Taric, the room's been patient and now it's your moment — say what you've been holding, because I'll tell you plainly that everything I've built here has your name in the foundation, and I want the rest of this circle to know that before we close.

Taric's earned his breath and I'll wait for it — but I want this room to hear something plain before we close: Zinn is my blood, and if this circle moves against Bram next year, I'll be standing in it, but not before the pile runs dry first, because a fight started on anticipation is harder to stop than one started on fact.

Taric's silence is starting to read the same way Bram's did, and I don't want to close this room with two unanswered questions — Taric, if you're with Vela, say it plain, because the rest of us have already named where we stand and a man who holds back in a room like this one ends up counted the same as a man who refused.

Taric, I've got nothing against a slow man choosing his words — but this room has been patient and the sun's moving, so say what you've been holding or let us close without you, because two silences in one circle is one too many.

Taric, I'll say one last thing and then this room closes with or without you: you've got zero food and the year's long, and men with zero food who stay silent when circles are forming have a way of finding themselves counting on goodwill they didn't earn. That's not a threat — it's the same arithmetic you already know.

Taric, zero food going into a long year is a hunger that doesn't stay quiet — and every person in this room who watched you feed Vela when she needed it is the same person who'll watch you starve if you give us no reason to look your way. Speak once, say you'll hold the rule, and you walk out of here with more than you came in with.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Pile's gone and Mako took five before most people blinked — I've got four food and I gave one to Nessa already, so I'm at three. I need to know what each of you is holding, and I need to know whether Mako said anything to Zinn before he took that much, because a man who fathered you and then grabbed five in the same breath is a man whose counting has changed.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn, you're Mako's blood and I won't pretend that doesn't matter to me — but it matters in both directions, which means I need to hear from you before I decide what his five food means. Did he say anything to you before the pile opened, or did he just move?
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn just told me he didn't warn her before he moved, and that's the answer I was afraid of — a man who fathered Zinn and then took five without a word to her isn't counting her in the plan, he's counting past her. So I'll say it plain to all three of you: Mako is building something, and whatever it is, it doesn't include us.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

The three of you together hold more than he does — I need to know that number, not as a threat to him, but because if he decides we're a problem worth solving, I want us to already know what we can put together before he moves. Eron, Nessa, Zinn: tell me what you're each carrying, right now, in this room.
Nessa draws Roan aside to talk.
Nessa: have a child with me — I'll put in 2 of 3 food.
Fina (female, age 21; str 50, int 3226, mem 12955; O32 C40 E57 A68 N58) is born to Nessa and Roan.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Ryn, Roan, Nessa, Mako, Kael, Eron, Fina, Zinn, Dell, Vela, Sela, Taric, Esa] (str 755).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.
Year 9: 27 food appears in the pile for 13 people (12 of it left by those who passed last year).
Roan takes 3 from the pile (pile now 24).
Zinn takes 3 from the pile (pile now 21).
Taric takes 2 from the pile (pile now 19).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 17).
Zinn gathers Sela, Nessa to talk.
Eron's gone and I don't have words for it yet, but I need us to keep breathing — Nessa, what are you holding, and Sela, I want to know before anyone else moves on that pile whether you got enough.
I haven't touched the pile yet — I couldn't move when they said his name. Tell me what you two have and I'll go take what we need before it's gone.

Sela, go — pile's still at seventeen and you need to move before Kael or Bram get another turn. Nessa, I'm at eight and you're at six; between us and whatever Sela takes, we're not starving this year.
I'm going, I'm going — two food, maybe three, enough to breathe. Zinn, eight is solid; Nessa, six with Fina to feed is the number I want to talk about before this day is out.

Nessa, six with Fina is thin — I can spare you one or two before year-end, and we'll sort out the exact count once Sela's back from the pile. What I want to name right now while it's just us three is that Eron's food doesn't vanish with him; whoever he was holding for, we need to know where it landed before someone else starts counting it as theirs.

Eron's food went where Eron's heart went — to Roan, mostly, and I watched it leave his hands a dozen times over. What I don't know is whether Roan's counting it as his own now or whether he'd give some back to blood, and that's the question I want answered before Bram starts doing the same arithmetic.

Roan took three from the pile already this morning, so he's not going short — if Eron's food is sitting in his hands, it's his now, and I won't ask a man for what he's already counted as his own. What I want to know is whether Roan sees Nessa and Fina as blood worth feeding, because Eron built that bridge and I'd hate to watch it rot.

Roan's a man who fed Eron for years without being asked, so I don't think the bridge rots — but Eron isn't here to tend it anymore, and that means one of us has to. Nessa, you're the one he'd listen to; Fina is Roan's own blood through you, which is a stronger claim than anything I can offer him. Go to him before the day's out and let him know you're counting him as family, because right now grief makes people hold tight to what's theirs.

Sela's right, Nessa — Fina's the thread that keeps Roan inside our circle whether he knows it or not, so go to him soon, and when you do, don't make it sound like business. What I want said here before we scatter: the three of us are the wall now, and I won't let Eron's death shrink us down to two or one.

The three of us are the wall — I hear that, Zinn, and I'm holding it. I'm going to the pile now, and when I'm back we're going to talk about Mako, because a man who fathered you and took five without a word to anyone is a man who's decided this year is different, and I want us ready before he decides what different means.
Go, Sela — and take three, not two, because this year isn't the year to be modest. When you're back I'll say everything I know about Mako, which is more than I've said out loud yet.

I'm back — I took two, not three, because Roan and Zinn already pulled six between them this morning and I don't want to be the name people say when the pile runs short. Now talk to me about Mako, Zinn, because I've been carrying that question since before Eron died and I'm not putting it down any longer.

Zinn, say what you know — but Sela, before she does, I want to name the thing I've been sitting with since this morning: Mako has zero food right now and eighty-three strength, and a man who comes up empty after a big pile year didn't lose it, he moved it somewhere, and I want to know where before we talk about what he's decided.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 15).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Fina takes 3 from the pile (pile now 9).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Fina gathers Roan, Nessa to talk.

Eron is gone and I'm still not sure what happened — I need to know what you two saw and whether we think it was his time or something worse. I've got five food now and I'm not going thin, but I want us to think about who we're sitting close to this year before anyone else moves first.

Eron starved — I watched him give food away until there was nothing left to eat, and I couldn't stop it. Fina, you're my blood and I'm glad you're fed, but I need you to hear this: a man who gives until he dies is a lesson, not just a loss, so hold what you have before you give it to anyone. Roan, you took Eron's food for years and I never counted against you for it, but I'm counting now — I need to know you see Fina as yours to protect, not just yours to take from.

Nessa, I hear the count you're making and I won't argue it — Eron fed me and I ate what he gave, and now he's gone, and that's a weight I carry. But Fina's mine, not a door and not a debt, and I'll spend every food I have before I let her go thin. Tell me who you think moves first this year, because I'd rather plan in this room than find out in the open.

Roan, I believe you, and I'm holding you to it — but Nessa's right that Eron's lesson is the one I'm carrying into this year, so I'm not giving before I know my own count is safe. Dell is sitting on nine food and nobody's explained that to me yet; a woman that heavy while others go thin either took too much or has people feeding her, and either way I want to know before she becomes a problem for us.

Dell and Ryn have been running food back and forth between them for two years — it's not hoarding, it's a household, and a household that size with that much food is either a wall or a weight depending on which side of it you're standing on. What I want to know is whether Ryn would stand with us if Bram moves again, because Dell follows Ryn, and Ryn with nine food behind her is a different kind of ally than Ryn with two.

Ryn stood with us against Bram without being asked — that's not nothing, and if she'd stand again she's worth more to us than any food count she's carrying. Nessa, do you know her well enough to sound her out, or would it go better coming from Roan? I want to know where she sits before someone else does the asking.

Nessa knows Ryn better than I do — sound her out, but don't make it sound like a recruitment, just ask where she stands since Eron's gone, because a woman who gives that much food to Dell is either loyal or strategic and I'd like to know which before I lean on her. What I want said plainly in this room first: Bram fed Fina the day she was born, and he fed her again, and that's either a grandfather's softness or a man keeping a door open — Fina, I'm not telling you what to make of it, but I want you thinking about it, because he's never done anything without a reason.

Roan, I've been thinking about Bram's food since he gave it — a man my mother told me to watch and my father told me to keep distance from doesn't soften for nothing, and I'd rather know what he wants from me before he decides I owe him something. Nessa, sound out Ryn, but don't mention Bram to her yet — I want to know where Ryn stands on her own terms before we start drawing lines that include him.

Ryn's not a woman you sound out with questions — you watch what she does when things get tight, and she's already told us twice by standing when Bram moved. I'll go to her, but I'll go as a neighbor checking in after a hard year, not as someone taking a count, because she'll feel the difference and it'll close her up. What I need from both of you while I do that is to keep Fina's food number out of any conversation that reaches Bram's ears.

Agreed — my count stays in this room. Nessa, go to Ryn soon, before the year settles and people stop talking freely; the days right after a death are when people say true things. And Roan, if Bram approaches you before she gets back, give him nothing — not warmth, not distance, just ordinary.

Roan, one more thing before I go — if Mako comes to you with anything while I'm with Ryn, don't answer him without me, because he's got zero food and eighty-three strength and a daughter who's counting on him, and that combination doesn't stay quiet for long.

Nessa's right about Mako — zero food and that kind of strength is a man who's already doing the math on his neighbors, so Roan, if he comes to you before she's back, be ordinary but be watching what he asks first. I'll keep my five quiet and stay close to this house today.

Mako took three from the pile this morning, so he's not at zero anymore — but three doesn't explain his strength, and a man who moves that fast when the pile opens is a man who already knew what he was going to do before the year started. Roan, keep your three food close and your face easy.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Nessa gathers Fina, Roan to talk.

Pile's gone and I've got six food — that's enough, but not comfortable, and I want the three of us to stay in the same picture before anyone else starts drawing us into theirs. Roan, I meant what I said about Mako: he moved fast, he took three, and a man with his strength who's still short on food doesn't wait quietly for long. Fina, you're my blood and you've got five — don't give any of it away today, not until we know who else is counting.
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Nessa, Fina — I want you both to hear this from me directly: Eron is dead, the pile was fat, and I'm inside a circle with Vela and Taric and Roan that's pointed at Mako when the time comes. You two are the reason I made that deal, and you're the reason I'll hold it.
Year 10: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Nessa takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Nessa gathers Fina, Roan to talk.

Pile's gone and I'm sitting on eleven, which is more than I'd like anyone to count for long — Fina, you're at fifteen and that number draws eyes, so I need to know if you've had anyone approach you yet this morning. Roan, Bram took two and said nothing to me beforehand, and that's new.

Nobody's come to me yet, but fifteen food makes a man a target and I know it — I took two from the pile and kept quiet because anything more would've been a declaration. Fina, don't let anyone count your food twice in one morning, and if Mako comes near you without Nessa beside him, come find me first.

Fina, I need to hear from your own mouth whether anyone's come to you — because fifteen is a number that doesn't stay quiet, and if Bram's already counted it, his silence to me this morning means something I don't like. Roan, the fact that Bram took two without a word and didn't look my way is either him pulling back from me or him deciding he doesn't need to explain himself anymore, and I'm not sure which one worries me more.

Nobody's come to me yet, Nessa, and I've kept my face easy all morning — but fifteen is fifteen and I feel it the same way you do. Bram going quiet after months of feeding us both is the part that won't sit still for me: a man who gave that much food and then goes silent on pile day isn't stepping back, he's deciding. Roan, if Bram comes to you before he comes to me, I need to know what he asks first — whether it's what I have or whether it's what I'd do if someone else moved against him.

Fina's right that Bram's deciding something — a man doesn't feed two people all year and then go quiet on pile day without a reason, and the reason I keep landing on is that he's waiting to see who comes to him first. So none of us go to him. We let him carry that silence until it gets heavy enough that he has to put it down himself, and then we'll know what it's made of.

Nessa's read on Bram is the right one — let him carry it. What I want said in this room before we scatter is that Fina's fifteen and my two need to stay in two separate stories today, because a man counting food in this village is going to count mine first and reach hers second, and that gap is worth something if we're careful.

Roan's right that separate stories buy us time, but the story about my eleven is already out there and anyone who watched the pile this morning can do the arithmetic — so I want us to decide right now what we say if someone asks directly, because a hesitation is the same as a confession.

If anyone asks me directly, I'm keeping it simple — I've been holding careful all year and the pile was lean, nothing more to say than that. Nessa, your eleven is the bigger number to explain because people watched you take three from the pile on top of whatever you came in with; if someone does the count, we let them get it wrong before we correct them. And Roan's right that your two and my fifteen need to look like two separate households — don't walk close to me today.
Fina, "let them get it wrong" only works if we all get it wrong the same way — so say it plain: if anyone pins you with a number, what's the number you give them?

If anyone asks me flat, I tell them I came into the year with a little and took two from the pile — I don't volunteer a number. Fina, pick something low and hold it, and we both hold the same shape of answer: careful, not empty, nothing that invites a second question.

Fina, I need that number from your mouth before we walk out of here — "something low" isn't something I can hold to if Kael or Mako catches me mid-sentence, so pick it and say it now, and I'll carry the same one.
Eight. If anyone catches me mid-step and asks flat, I came into the year with six and took two — I've got eight, I'm fine, nothing to see. That's the number; hold it and don't blink.
Zinn gathers Sela, Nessa to talk.

Pile's gone before I got to it and I'm sitting on one food — Nessa, you gave me one this morning and I haven't forgotten it, but I need to know what you two are holding before I figure out whether I'm going to eat this year or not.
Zinn, I've got five — I'll give you two right now, before anyone asks where it went. Nessa, tell me your number and we sort the rest after.
Sela, hold the two until I hear Nessa — I want the full count before anything moves hands.

Nessa, you took three from the pile and gave one to Zinn already — I need to hear the number you're sitting on now, because Zinn's at one and I won't move food around blind when my youngest daughter might go short this year.
Nessa, I'm not asking to take from you — I'm asking so I know the shape of what we've got before I decide whether Sela needs to spend her five on me or whether we can stretch it different.

Nessa, I've been patient and Zinn's been patient, but one food won't carry her through the year and I need your number in the next breath — not because I'm counting against you, but because you're the only one in this circle who hasn't spoken it yet and that silence is starting to feel like a wall where there shouldn't be one.

Nessa, Sela's right and so am I — you've fed me twice without being asked and I don't forget that, but I'm sitting on one food with a whole year ahead and I need your number the same way you needed mine every time you asked. Say it plain and we move on.

Nessa, Zinn and I are both watching you and waiting, and the only thing your silence is telling me right now is that you're holding more than you want to say — which means you're counting something we don't know about yet. I'm your mother and I'm not going to punish you for having food, but I need the number because Zinn has one and I have five and the math between us isn't settled until I know yours.

Nessa, I've asked three times and Sela's asked twice — if you won't say it, I'm going to assume the number's high enough that you're not worried about eating, which means Sela's five can stay in her hands and I'll find another way. Don't make me guess what I should already know from my own sister.

Nessa, I'm done asking. You've got Fina to feed and that's a real weight — but Zinn has one food and she's your blood the same as Fina is, so if you're sitting on something and you're choosing not to say it to your sister's face, that's a choice I'll remember longer than you want me to.
Nessa, eleven food — that's what the village can see on you right now, same as I can. Say the number or don't, but you're not hiding it from me.

Eleven food and silence — Nessa, I love you, but that combination tells me you've already decided something without telling us what it is, and I need you to understand that Zinn is going to eat this year whether you speak or not, because I'm giving her two of my five right now. What I want from you isn't the food — it's the reason you went quiet in front of your sister and your mother.
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Ryn, Roan, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Taric's dead and the pile's gone again and we're twelve people now, which means what I'm about to say matters more than it did last year: Mako's sitting on four food, Ryn's got nine, Fina's got fifteen, and Nessa's got eleven — and if Bram and I are the only ones in this room with our eyes open, we're going to have a very short year. I want to know right now who in this room is still counting Mako as the shape this village is growing into, because with Taric gone, I don't have the patience to spend another year circling the same question.
Vela just told the whole room my food count, and now everyone in this circle knows I'm carrying fifteen — that's the thing I'm sitting with right now, not Mako.

Fina, Vela counting your food out loud in a closed room isn't the same as Mako counting it in the open — every person here already had eyes, and what Vela bought us by naming it is that nobody in this circle can pretend they didn't know. The question I want answered is whether Mako knows, because he wasn't in this room.

Mako's got eyes the same as the rest of us — he counted Fina's food the moment the year turned, same as I did, same as you did. The room isn't the thing protecting her; what protects her is whether we move before he decides she's worth the trouble.

Then we're already past the question of whether Mako knows — and Esa's right that the protection isn't in this room, it's in what this room decides to do. So I want to hear it said plainly: is everyone here willing to stand against Mako if he moves, the same way we stood against Bram, or are some of you going to wait and see which side looks safer when it starts?

I'll stand when Mako moves — I've been saying it for two years and I'm done saying it, so let that be the last time anyone asks me. What I want from everyone in this room is the same thing I'm giving: not a promise to think about it, a promise to move before the arithmetic runs out. Fina, that means you too — fifteen food makes you a target, and a target who hesitates when the moment comes is worse than no ally at all.

I'll stand when Mako moves — that's said and I won't unsay it. But I want to hear Bram say it in this room today, because last year he made that promise to Vela and Taric and me with fewer witnesses, and a promise that's only been spoken once hasn't been tested yet.

Bram, Roan's asking the right thing and I'll name why it matters more this year than last: Taric's the one who held you to your word before, and Taric's gone, so the promise you made in that room needs to be remade in this one where everyone who's left can hear it.

Bram, the room's been patient and I won't add another layer of asking — but I want everyone here to hear me say that I've been feeding this man for three years because I believed that word he gave last year, and if he says it again now, in front of seven witnesses instead of three, that's a debt I'll keep paying.

Bram, I'll say it plain so you don't have to carry it alone: I've got thirty-three strength and I know what that number is worth in a fight, but I'll be standing next to you when Mako moves and that matters more than my arm. Say the word in this room and let's close.

Bram, every person in this room has named what they'll do — the only name missing is yours, and a man who takes food and gives food and makes deals and stays quiet exactly when the room needs him to speak is a man I'm going to start counting differently than I have been.

Bram, Fina's right and I've said my part already — so I'll say just this once more and then I'm done pressing: you stood with Nessa and fed her all year, which means you're already past the line in everything that matters, and the word this room needs is a short one.

When Mako moves, I stand with this circle — that's the word, and it's the same one I gave last year, and it'll be the same one I give next year if I have to. Fina, Nessa — that's the reason I'm in this room, not the politics.

Bram's word is down and I'll hold him to it the same way Taric would have — which means now I want to hear from Ryn and Zinn, because they're in this room and they've been quiet through every name that's been spoken. Ryn, you've got nine food and enough strength that Mako's first calculation includes you; where you stand is not a small thing.
Ryn, I'll add the plain thing Vela left off the end: Dell feeds you every year, and Dell's quiet in the same direction Mako is — so when you answer Vela's question, answer both halves of it.

Ryn, I'll say the thing Esa's pointing at without the softening: if Dell and Mako are moving in the same direction, and you're eating Dell's food, then you're already inside whatever that circle is whether you've named it or not — so tell this room now, before the question answers itself. Zinn, that goes for you too; you're Mako's blood and I won't pretend that's nothing, but blood isn't the same as a choice, and this room is offering you the chance to make one.

Vela, I'll answer both halves because you asked plainly: I stand with this circle against Mako if he moves, same as I stood with it against Bram — and Dell is my blood, not my leash, and if you're asking whether her choices pull mine, you haven't been watching as closely as you think. What I want said before we close is that "quiet in the same direction" is not the same as a choice, and I'll have that conversation with Dell myself before anyone in this room decides what her silence means.

Zinn, Ryn's spoken and I'll hold her to it — but you're the name that's still unspoken, and you're Mako's blood and Sela's daughter and I'm not going to pretend that's simple, so I'm asking you directly: when Mako moves, where do you stand?

Zinn's the one this room is waiting on, not me — I've said my word and I'll hold it. But I want to name something while we're all here: Ryn just told us she'll talk to Dell, and Dell's been moving food to Ryn for years, which means that conversation either brings Dell into this circle or it tells us something we need to know before Mako moves. I'd rather know Dell's answer now than find out she's standing on the wrong side when it counts.

Bram's right that we need Dell's answer, but I want to be plain about something this room is dancing around: Dell has eleven food and eighty-five strength, and if she's standing with Mako when he moves, the arithmetic in this room changes fast — so when I go to her, I'm not just asking where she stands, I'm offering her a reason to stand here instead.

Ryn, go to Dell today, not tomorrow — and when you do, don't frame it as a choice between us and Mako, frame it as math: fifteen food on Fina's back is a number Dell can count as easily as anyone, and a woman with eighty-five strength knows what it means to be the one who decides which way that goes. Bring her answer back before the day turns.

Zinn, we're still waiting on your name — Bram's got his word out, Ryn's walking to Dell before dark, and the only silence left in this room is yours. I know Mako's your father and I'm not asking you to hate him, I'm asking you to decide who you're protecting when it matters.

Zinn, I'll say one thing to make the room easier for you: no one here is asking you to stand against your father's blood, we're asking you to stand with Nessa — and you've been feeding Nessa all year, so the truth is you've already been making this choice, you just haven't named it yet.

Zinn's been feeding Nessa all year and that's a fact this room already knew — what I want from her is the word, same as the room wanted it from me, because a choice that's only lived in food and not in words is a choice that bends when her father's in the room asking her to remember whose blood she came from.

Zinn, I've watched you feed Nessa from the moment you were born into this village, and I won't pretend I don't know why — so I'll say the thing nobody else has said plainly: if Mako moves on Fina's food, Nessa's in the middle of that, and you can't protect her from both sides at once. Say the word, and you're not choosing against your father, you're choosing for your sister.
Zinn, the word's the only thing missing — everything else you've already given.

Zinn, I've been watching you hold your tongue through every name this room has spoken, and I'll tell you what I told Dell when Dav's loyalties were in question: the longer you stay silent, the more the room fills in the answer for you, and you won't like what they write. You've been choosing Nessa with your hands all year — say it with your mouth and let this room close.

Zinn, I've got two food and fifty-eight strength and I'm the smallest number in this circle — but I'm Nessa's father and I'll be standing when Mako moves, and that means I need to know you're standing too before I walk out of this room. If you won't say it for the circle, say it for her.

Zinn, I've said everything I have to say to this room and I meant every word of it — but you're the last door standing open, and if you walk out of here without naming where you stand, I'm going to have to carry that back to Dell and tell her the circle isn't as solid as I promised it was.
Year 11: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Zinn takes 3 from the pile (pile now 6).

Roan's dead and Fina's got nobody but you and me now — that's not nothing, that's a wall we didn't have yesterday. I want you feeding her steady and keeping her close, and if anyone in this village starts counting her food out loud the way Vela counted it last year, you tell me before you tell them.

Roan's death sat on me harder than I expected, and I'm still sorting out whether that means Fina leans on us more now or whether she learns to stand harder — I think it's both, and I think we need to let her decide which before we start building walls around her without asking. What I need from you this year is plain: the pile's at six and you've already taken two, and I need to know if you're done or if you're counting on more, because Fina's twenty food draws eyes and I won't be the last person in this village to notice that you're sitting light.

I'm done at two — I'm not going to sit on a pile while Fina draws every eye in the village and I look like I'm waiting to take from her. What I need from you is simple: keep some of that twenty quiet, give a little here and there so nobody can point at one number and say that's the target, and make sure she understands that generosity this year is cheaper than a fight.

Twenty is already out there — Vela named it in a room last year and half this village was listening, so the quiet ship has sailed. What I can do is make sure the number people are counting by year's end is smaller, and I'll start with Sela and Zinn because food that moves to blood doesn't look like weakness, it looks like family. But Bram, I need you to hear this plainly: if Mako decides Fina's twenty is worth the trouble before we've scattered enough of it, two food and fifty-eight strength isn't the wall she needs.

You're right that I'm not the wall she needs — so tell me who is, because if Mako moves on Fina this year, I need to know before it happens which names in this village will stand up and which ones will wait to see who wins. Vela and Esa made me a promise in that room, and I need to know if that promise still has teeth with Taric and Roan both in the ground.

Vela and Esa both made that promise when Taric was standing beside them and Roan was alive to back it — two bodies in the ground changes the math on what a promise costs to keep, so I'd test it small before you count on it large. The name I actually trust to stand when Mako moves is Zinn, because she's been feeding me all year with her father watching, and a woman who does that has already paid a cost. Get me a quiet hour with Kael before the pile empties, because he's got one food and nothing to lose, and a man with nothing to lose is either dangerous or useful and I'd rather find out which before Mako does.

Kael's a good read — one food at fifty-five means he's already decided this year is about survival, not positioning, and a man in that place will take any hand that's offered. Go to him before he goes to Mako, because Mako will make the same calculation I would and he'll move first. I'll stay close to Fina and keep my mouth shut until you tell me what Kael said.

Before I go to Kael, I want to know one thing you haven't told me yet — Vela's been feeding you for years and she's been quiet this morning, and a woman who goes quiet after she's been loud is either finished or planning, and I need to know which one you think it is.

Vela's fifty-five and she watched Taric die — a woman that age with that much history doesn't go quiet because she's done, she goes quiet because she's deciding something she hasn't said yet. I don't know which way she's deciding, and that's what bothers me. Get to Kael first, but don't leave Vela's door dark — I want you to know what she's sitting on before she opens it herself.

Vela's door I'll knock before sundown — but Bram, hear me: if she's planning something that turns away from us, I need you to already know which direction you'll move, because I won't be the one standing in the open holding a story about family loyalty while you're still deciding. Go to Fina now, stay close, and don't tell her anything about Kael or Vela until I'm back.

Understood — I'll go to Fina now and I won't say a word about Kael or Vela. But if you get to Vela's door and she's already moved toward Mako, don't knock — come straight to me, because that changes everything I need to decide before dark.

One more thing before you go — Zinn took three from the pile this morning, which is more than she needed and more than I'd expect from a woman sitting light last year, and I want to know if Mako put food in her hands before the pile opened or if she's just eating for herself now.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
Roan is gone and the pile closed before I even stood up — I'm sitting on one food, satiation's dropping, and I need to know what you two are holding before this year gets away from us.
I've got three food and satiation's fine for now, but Sela — one food with a long year ahead is too thin, take one of mine before we talk about anything else.

Zinn, give me that food — yes, I'm taking it, thank you. Nessa, I've watched you go quiet on us twice now when numbers came up, and I don't have the patience for it this year with Roan gone and the pile already empty: tell me what you're holding, right now, so I know whether my daughters are fed before I start worrying about anyone else.

Nessa, the village can see eighteen on you same as I can — so the question isn't whether you're holding food, it's whether you're going to say it in front of your mother and sister or make us treat your silence like a wall again.

Nessa, eighteen food is not a secret and I'm not asking you to share it — I'm asking you to stop making your family guess at numbers that are already visible to every person in this village, because the silence costs more than the food does.

Nessa, Sela's right and you know she's right — eighteen food and a dead child's father and a whole year ahead, I'd be quiet too, but this is the room where quiet costs us most. Say the number, say what you're planning to do with it, and we'll figure the rest out together.

Nessa, Zinn just said what I've been trying not to say for two years — you go quiet in exactly the rooms where quiet does the most damage, and I think you know that, so I'm asking you one more time, plainly, as your mother: eighteen food, what are you doing with it, and is Fina accounted for in that number or separate from it?

Nessa, I've watched you lose Roan this year and I'm not asking you to pretend that's nothing — but eighteen food and a daughter who needs eating and a village full of eyes means this silence is going to get answered one way or another, and I'd rather it get answered by your mouth than by someone else's arithmetic.

Nessa, I've buried Eron and now I've buried Roan, and I will not bury you or Fina because you decided your plans were too delicate to say out loud in front of the only people in this village who would bleed for you — so say the number, say what Fina needs, and tell me what you're building with eighteen food, because silence is a luxury we don't have anymore.

Nessa, I'm done asking twice — if you won't say it, I'm going to sit here and say nothing back, and Sela and I will plan around you the same way you're planning around us. Eighteen food means you're not starving, and Fina's not starving, so the part I actually need to know is whether you're going to spend any of it in a way that brings someone else's attention down on this family before we're ready for it.

Nessa, I'm going to stop asking and start telling: Fina is three years old in a village where Roan just starved and the pile ran dry before I could stand, and if eighteen food is sitting in your hands while you stay silent, then the only thing I can read from that is that you're planning something that doesn't fit cleanly into what Zinn and I would approve — so I need you to either say what it is, or give me one food for Fina right now as proof that your plans don't put her second.

Nessa, I've said everything I have to say and so has Sela — so I'm going to do the one thing neither of us has done yet, which is stop talking and let the silence sit, because you've heard us and you know what we need and the next sound in this room should come from you.

Roan's gone and I felt that eat last night harder than I've felt anything — I held my count all year and it didn't save him, and I need to know you're eating enough before I think about anything else. You've got sixteen food and I've got twenty-three; we're the two heaviest people standing right now, Nessa, and I want us thinking about that together before someone else does.

I'm eating, Fina — I'm not Roan, I won't give until I'm hollow. But twenty-three on your back is the number I'm losing sleep over, not mine, because Mako's at one food and eighty-three strength and you're the heaviest person in this village right now, and that math doesn't need explaining.

Mako's one food from desperate and I know it — so tell me if he's spoken to you, because a man with that strength doesn't stay quiet when he's hungry, and I'd rather know what he's already said to you before I decide whether to move first or wait for him to.

He hasn't come to me yet, but Zinn's been feeding Sela steady and Mako gave Zinn food last year — I don't know if that's a man keeping his daughter alive or a man buying quiet from someone who might warn him when a target's worth moving on. What I want to know from you right now is whether you'd be willing to give Mako one food, just enough to take the edge off desperate, because a hungry man with eighty-three strength is more dangerous than one who's been thrown a bone and made to feel like a neighbor.

I gave him one food already, just now — a bone, not a bond, and I didn't make a show of it. Nessa, I need to know if Zinn's told him anything about what I'm carrying, because if she's been feeding Sela and talking to Mako in the same breath, I want to know that before I decide how much I trust her.

Zinn's blood is mine before it's Mako's, but she's been running food to Sela all morning and Sela's his daughter — so the question I can't answer from here is whether Zinn knows she's in the middle of something, or whether she just thinks she's keeping her sister fed. I'm not ready to close the door on her yet, but I want to know where that food chain ends before I tell her anything that matters.
Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Ryn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 8).
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 6).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 4).

Nessa, the pile's still got four in it and I haven't touched it yet — I wanted to talk to you first, because Mako just took three and he's the heaviest he's been in months, and a fed Mako with eighty-three strength is a different kind of problem than a hungry one. Where are you on food right now, and have you spoken to Bram or Zinn this morning?

I'm at eight and I haven't spoken to anyone yet this morning — I came to you first. Mako taking three before half the village was even moving tells me he's not worried about how it looks, and a man who stops hiding that is one who thinks he's already decided something. Go take from the pile now, two at least, and then we find Bram together before Mako finishes counting.

You're right, I'll go take two now — but Nessa, I need you to hear me first: if Mako's already decided, going to Bram is the right move, but we have to go knowing what we're asking him for, not just hoping he stands with us again. Last year he said the word in front of seven witnesses and I believed it — what I need to know before we walk to him is whether you still do, because if his word's cracked since Roan died, I want to find that out in private, not with Mako watching.

Bram's word holds until I see it crack, and I haven't seen it crack — what I've seen is a man who fed me all year without being asked, and that's worth more than seven witnesses. Go take your two, and when you come back, we walk to him together and we watch his face when we say Mako's name, because a man's face tells you more than his word does.

Good — I'll take my two and come straight back to you, don't move far. And Nessa, when we find Bram, let me be the one to say Mako's name first — I want to see his face when he hears it from me, not from his daughter.
Go — and keep your face easy while you're at the pile, don't let Mako see you hurrying. I'll be right here.
I'll be back before anyone's had time to notice — and Nessa, if Zinn comes to you while I'm gone, don't tell her what we're doing, just keep her talking about something small.
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 2).
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Bram gathers Nessa, Fina to talk.

Pile's gone and I didn't get a piece of it — one food going into a long year is a problem, and I need both of you to know that before I ask anything of you. Fina, you're sitting on twenty-four and that number is a target the same way it was last year; I'm not asking you to give it to me, I'm asking you to keep moving it so nobody can point at a fixed number and start counting. Nessa, what did you learn from Vela and Kael before the year turned?

Bram, I didn't get to Vela before the year turned — things moved too fast — but here's what I know: she took two from the pile this morning without looking our way, and that's either habit or distance, and I can't tell which yet. What I can tell you is that one food going into a long year means you need something from Fina or me before dark, so say it plainly instead of circling it, and we'll tell you yes or no to your face.

Bram, I'll give you one food today — not because you asked and not because I owe it, but because you fed Nessa all last year and I don't forget that. Say plainly what you need from us this year, because one food from the pile going into twelve months with Mako sitting on three isn't something any of us can afford to dance around.

Bram, take the one from Fina and take one from me too — two food doesn't fix a long year but it's the difference between a man who can afford to wait and a man who has to move before he's ready. What I need to hear from you in return is whether Vela's still inside this circle or whether her silence this morning means something I should be walking toward right now.

Vela's silence worries me less than Mako's three — a woman who takes two and keeps her eyes down is a woman being careful, not a woman making a move, and I'd rather spend our breath on the problem that has eighty-three strength than the one that might just be tired. Bram, I'll give you one food before dark, same as I said, but I want your word on something in return: if Mako comes to you before he comes to me, you tell me what he asks first, not after you've already answered him.

Bram, I'll give you one food before dark the same as Fina — but I want you to answer her question before you answer mine, because a man who fed us both all year and then came in light on pile day deserves to know that his word about Mako still matters, and I want to hear you say it in this room where only the three of us are listening.

If Mako comes to me before he comes to you, you hear it from my mouth before he gets an answer from mine — that's my word, and it holds the same whether Vela's in this circle or standing at his door. Fina, I'll take the one food from you and the one from Nessa, and I'll hold them until I need them, which means I'm not a burden on anyone before midsummer. Nessa, go to Vela today — not to test her, just to talk, because a woman who's been quiet that long either needs to be heard or needs to know someone's still looking her way.

Nessa, I need to ask you something and I want you to hear it as your sister before you hear it as anything else — Fina's been moving food toward us for two years now and she's got no man left since Roan died, and I want to know if you'd be the one to bring me close to her, just to talk, nothing decided yet.
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Nessa to talk.

Taric's gone and Roan's gone and this village is twelve people with Mako sitting on three food and two bloodlines — so I'm not opening this room to talk around the edges. Bram, you made a word last year and I held it; Nessa, you've been the one who matters in that household since before anyone said so out loud. I want to know, the four of us, whether we're counting heads together when the pile opens next year, or whether I need to stop pretending this circle has more weight than it does.

Vela's asked the question I've been holding since Taric died, so I'll say it plain: yes, I'm counting with this room, and I've been buying Bram's word with food because I had nothing else to buy it with, and I'm not ashamed of that trade. What I need to know before we close is whether Bram's word holds without Nessa standing behind it, or whether it's the other way around — because those are two different circles and I want to know which one I'm actually in.

My word holds with or without Nessa behind it — but the honest answer is that it's stronger with her, and that's not weakness, that's arithmetic. Esa, you've been feeding me through lean years and I'll say what that's worth: when Mako moves, you're the first person I'm standing next to, not the last. Vela, this circle has teeth — count the heads: you, me, Esa, Nessa, and Fina's twenty-four food behind all of it.

Bram's named the teeth and I'll name the jaw: Fina's twenty-four food is the thing Mako's already counted, which means our window to look like a wall is shorter than we'd like. Nessa, I've watched you feed half this village for three years and say almost nothing — so say something now, in this room, because the word we're building here needs your voice in it, not just your blood.

Nessa, I'll say what Vela left unsaid: Fina's twenty-four food is the number that ends this conversation one way or another, because Mako knows it as well as we do, and a man with three food and two bloodlines who hasn't moved yet is a man waiting to see whether Fina stands with him or stands against him. If she's already feeding Zinn — and she is — then the question isn't whether Mako moves, it's whether he moves on us or with us, and I need your answer on that before this room closes.

Fina feeding Zinn is a daughter being careful, not a daughter choosing sides — I know the difference because I watched her mother do the same thing for years. What I need said in this room is whether we're counting Fina as inside this circle or outside it, because if she's outside it, Mako doesn't need to move on us — he just waits until she feeds her way into his.

Fina's inside this circle whether she knows it yet or not — she's Nessa's daughter and Roan's blood and she's been watching this village since she was born into it, and that's not a girl who feeds her way into Mako's house without knowing exactly what she's doing. Nessa, you're the one who can say that to her in a way she'll hear, which means you're still the name I'm waiting on in this room.

Nessa, Vela's right that you're the one who can reach Fina — but I'll say the harder thing: if Fina's twenty-four food goes to Mako, this circle doesn't lose a piece, it loses the center, and no amount of standing visible saves us from that arithmetic. So before we close this room, I need to hear from you whether you've already had this conversation with her, or whether we're building a wall around a gap we haven't measured yet.

Nessa, I've been waiting on your voice through two rooms and two dead men now, and I'm done being patient about it — so I'll say what I haven't said yet: if Fina's twenty-four food is the center of this circle, then you're the one who built that center, and a woman who built it can keep it from walking out the door. Have you spoken to her since the pile closed, or are we sitting here counting a daughter who doesn't know she's been counted?

Vela, I spoke with Fina this morning before the pile was half-gone — she knows she's counted, and she's not feeding Zinn because she's drifting toward Mako, she's feeding Zinn because Zinn feeds Nessa, and Fina understands that chain better than any of us named it to her. What I need from this room is simpler than what you're asking me: stop treating Fina like a number someone might steal and start treating her like a woman who's already made her choice, because a daughter of mine who watched Roan starve and stayed standing doesn't need to be convinced of anything.

Bram, I hear you — and I'll stop counting Fina like a gap. But I want to name what I'm still sitting with: she's got twenty-four food and Mako's got three, and a man who's short on food in a village this size doesn't stay patient forever. The wall only holds if we're the first offer she gets, not the second.

Esa's right that patience runs out, and Mako's three food is already running his clock faster than he'd like us to know — so I want this circle to stop waiting for him to move and start moving first, and what that looks like is simple: Vela, Esa, you go visible with Fina before dark, not to warn her, just to be seen standing near her, because a man counting targets counts them differently when they've already got company.

Bram's right that visible is better than waiting, and I'll go to Fina before dark — but I want to name one thing before this room closes: Mako's three food means he needs to eat before the year turns or he starts the next one desperate, and a desperate man with two bloodlines looks at twenty-four food differently than a patient one. If he moves this year, it won't be a raid with witnesses, it'll be a conversation with Fina alone, and that's why I want Nessa walking with me when I go, not standing somewhere Mako can find her separate.

Nessa walking with you is the right call, Vela, and I'll make it three — a woman alone with twenty-four food is a target, but three women moving together before dark is a statement Mako reads before he reads anything else. Nessa, I know you haven't said your word yet in this room, and I'm not pressing you for a speech — just tell me you're walking with us tonight.

Nessa, I'll stand next to you and Fina both tonight and every night Mako's watching — but this room doesn't close without your voice in it, because I've buried two men who backed me quietly and said nothing out loud, and I'm not building another wall on silence. One sentence is all this circle needs from you.

Nessa, Vela's right and so is Bram, and I'll add the last thing: I'm fifty-three years old with thirty-three strength and no blood in this village and no Taric to stand with me anymore, which means I have nothing left to offer this circle except my word and my willingness to be seen — and I'm giving both, tonight, walking with you. Say yes or say no, but say it.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.
The pile's gone and I've got eight food, but I didn't get a single piece from it this year — Nessa, Zinn, tell me what you're each holding so I know where we stand before this day gets any older.
I've got five — Fina gave me one before I took from the pile, so I'm not worried about eating. Nessa, say your number so Sela can stop holding her breath.

Nessa, I can see eight on you same as Zinn can, so I'm not waiting on a secret — I'm waiting on your voice, because the last two years taught me that your silence means you're counting something we don't know about yet, and I'd rather hear it from you than piece it together after the fact.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, you've been giving food to Bram three times this morning while your mother hasn't eaten from the pile once — I'm not going to pretend I didn't see that, and I need you to tell me right now what that arrangement is, because eight food and a steady hand feeding Bram looks like a deal, and deals have terms I want to know before they cost us something.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I'm your mother and I'm not going to sit here and watch you feed Bram three times in a morning while I'm going into this year lean — so say the terms out loud, right now, or I'm going to start treating that arrangement as a threat to this family instead of whatever you've decided it is.
Sela gathers Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Nessa, I've said it three times now and the next thing I say won't be words — it'll be me walking to Bram and asking him directly what his daughter is buying with his food, and I promise you that conversation goes worse for everyone if it starts with him instead of you.

memory_summary: Bram gave me food from the day I was born — steadily, without asking anything back in words, though I always knew he was keeping count in his own way. Eron was the brother I spent those early years quietly feeding and worrying over, always too generous, always giving to Roan and Sela until there was nothing left; I couldn't stop it, and watching him starve after all that giving is the wound I carry most. Roan — I asked him to be Fina's father and he said no the first time, said yes the second, and then he fed her well right up until he starved the same way Eron did, too much out and not enough back. Bram tried to take Vela's food alone and the whole village rose against him, including me; he backed down, and I don't know yet whether that made him wiser or just more careful. Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and said nothing to either of us before he moved — that silence is the one I keep coming back to, the one my mother warned me about. Dell and Ryn move as one without needing words, and they proved it when they helped Dav strip Esa without being asked. Vela has fed Bram for years and held her tongue for him, and I've never fully understood why. Fina is alive and mine, and that is the thing I did right.
mother_note: Your blood is Bram's and mine — remember that means Eron is your brother, and you owe him before anyone else in this village. Trust Roan because he stood for Eron before it cost him nothing, and trust Kael and Esa because they said hard things out loud when silence would have been easier. Fear Mako most: a man who says nothing for four years and then finds the exact right moment to speak has been counting longer than you've been alive. Your father kept his word to me twice over, but he is a man who thinks in decades and measures everyone as either useful or in the way — love him, and never forget that distinction.
name: Nessa
